question: A 16-year-old boy with Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) is found to have elevated LH and FSH with low serum testosterone. Which of the following best explains this hormonal pattern?

answers.text: Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism due to impaired hypothalamic GnRH pulsatility

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (low LH/FSH + low testosterone) is seen in conditions like Kallmann syndrome, where hypothalamic GnRH secretion is impaired. In Klinefelter syndrome the hypothalamo-pituitary axis is intact — it is the testes (primary gonadal failure) that are defective.

answers.text: Hypergonadotropic hypogonadism due to primary testicular failure from seminiferous tubule dysgenesis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: In Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY), progressive fibrosis and hyalinisation of the seminiferous tubules leads to primary testicular failure. The testes cannot produce adequate testosterone or inhibin B, so negative feedback at the hypothalamus and pituitary is lost — LH and FSH rise (hypergonadotropic). The result is small, firm testes and androgen deficiency.

answers.text: Secondary hypogonadism due to pituitary adenoma compressing gonadotroph cells

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Pituitary adenoma causes secondary (central/hypogonadotropic) hypogonadism with low LH, low FSH, and low testosterone. This is a distinct entity from Klinefelter syndrome and would require different investigations and management.

answers.text: Androgen insensitivity resulting in elevated testosterone with low LH and FSH

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Complete androgen insensitivity syndrome (CAIS) presents in a 46,XY individual as phenotypic female; LH is elevated but FSH normal or low, and testosterone is in the male range. This is unrelated to Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) and the hormonal pattern is entirely different.

overallFeedback.feedback: In Klinefelter syndrome, the defect is at the level of the testes (primary), not the hypothalamus or pituitary. High LH + high FSH + low testosterone = hypergonadotropic hypogonadism. This distinguishes it from Kallmann syndrome (hypogonadotropic) and androgen insensitivity (elevated testosterone).

Correct. Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) causes hypergonadotropic hypogonadism: primary testicular failure (seminiferous tubule dysgenesis) → low testosterone and inhibin B → loss of negative feedback → elevated LH and FSH. Small, firm testes are the clinical hallmark.
